title: LIVE: Minneapolis - The Madd Gasser of Mattoon
summary: Live recording at the State Theater in Minneapolis of Stuff You Should Know covering the 1944 "Mad Gasser of Mattoon" mystery in Mattoon, Illinois. The hosts recount the September 1944 series of reported paralytic gas attacks, beginning with the Kearney household, the Journal Gazette's sensational front-page coverage, the strained local police department, the vigilante Anti Theft Association, the state investigators, Chief Cole's policy of stomach-contents testing, and the attacks' end. They then cover Donald Johnson's 1945 psychology paper attributing the episode to mass hysteria, the case against that conclusion, and Scott Marona's theory that Farley Llewellyn, a local chemist, was responsible. The episode ends without a solution.
topics: Illinois Bureau of Crime Identification and Investigation

entities.name: Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology

segments.title: Opening banter and Mattoon introduction
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck welcome the State Theater audience in Minneapolis and introduce Mattoon, Illinois, known for the Begel capital claim and the 1944 mad gasser story. Sponsor mention and banter.

segments.title: Mattoon in 1944
segments.summary: Description of Mattoon in 1944 as a small farming and railroad town of about sixteen thousand, with a Brown Shoe factory, and many young men away fighting World War II.

segments.title: The Kearney attack
segments.summary: On September 1, 1944, Aileen Kearney and her toddler Dorothy were overcome by a sweet-smelling gas that paralyzed them. Her sister Martha Reedy was present, neighbor Earl Robertson searched the yard, and police found nothing.

segments.title: Bert Kearney sighting and Journal Gazette headline
segments.summary: Bert Kearney, a cab driver, saw a tall prowler in a watch cap in the backyard and it fled. The next day Journal Gazette reporter John Miller ran a front-page headline about an anesthetic prowler, and the Urban and Pauline Raife attack a night earlier came to light.

segments.title: Further victims and physical evidence
segments.summary: More families came forward, including the Ryder family. Beula Cordis found a moist pink cloth and inhaled it, suffering bleeding and other effects. Further attacks occurred on September 5, including on Laura Jenkins, Viola Spangler, eleven-year-old Glenda Hendershot, and Fred Goebel, who was spotted fleeing.

segments.title: Town fear and newspaper headlines
segments.summary: Residents locked doors and windows. The Thursday paper ran another large headline. The Anti Theft Association vigilantes began roaming town with guns.

segments.title: Police commissioner and vigilante PSA
segments.summary: Police commissioner Thomas Wright said he would not walk his backyard at night for ten thousand dollars. The police issued a warning to citizens about shooting at prowlers.

segments.title: Understaffed and divided Mattoon police
segments.summary: The Mattoon police force had about ten officers, half of what was needed, and was split between loyalty to Thomas Wright and Chief Cole. Officers lacked two-way radios and vigilantes followed police to calls.

segments.title: State investigators and state patrol support
segments.summary: Illinois Bureau of Crime Identification and Investigation investigators Richard Piper and Francis Barry arrived, the FBI showed up to observe, and state patrol officers doubled the force and brought two-way radios.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Mid-show ad break.

segments.title: Suspect profile and chemical theories
segments.summary: Investigators profiled the attacker as mentally imbalanced and possibly a skilled chemist who used chloroform, chloropicrin, or a self-designed paralytic agent. Chief Cole suggested nerves.

segments.title: Movie theater case and carbon tetrachloride theory
segments.summary: Missus Fitzpatrick smelled gas at a movie theater, causing a stampede, but was not gassed. Chief Cole blamed carbon tetrachloride fumes from the Atlas Imperial Diesel Engine Company, which denied it and cited a health inspector.

segments.title: Journal Gazette editorial and aside
segments.summary: The Journal Gazette wrote an editorial criticizing Chief Cole for not taking the case seriously and revealing the department's habit of covering up crimes. Short aside about the live recording.

segments.title: Investigation of suspects and national press
segments.summary: Police examined about thirty people, including state hospital records. The story spread to Chicago and St. Louis papers and internationally. A soldier in Papua New Guinea was quoted, and a mad scientist remark was reported and denied.

segments.title: Stomach-tube policy and final attacks
segments.summary: On September 10, Chief Cole announced that callers would either be taken to hospital for stomach contents testing or spend a night in jail. The last recorded attack was on September 11 at Bertha Bentz's home, involving a short, stout prowler and a high heel print.

segments.title: Calls drop off and Mattoon-Decatur feud
segments.summary: The attacks stopped, state patrol left, and the Journal Gazette stopped covering the story. A newspaper feud with Decatur, Illinois followed.

segments.title: Total attacks and skeptics
segments.summary: Chuck estimates about twenty-four attacks and roughly twenty-eight people affected. Journal Gazette went quiet and Chief Cole called the affair a mistake from beginning to end.

segments.title: Donald Johnson's mass hysteria study
segments.summary: Student Donald Johnson from the University of Illinois studied the victims using a homemade socioeconomic scale based on schooling, age, sex, occupation, income, and household conveniences. He concluded the episode was psychogenic mass hysteria.

segments.title: Johnson paper publication and ad break
segments.summary: Johnson's paper was published in the January 1945 Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, making Mattoon a textbook case of mass hysteria. Ad break follows.
topics: Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology

segments.title: Case for mass hysteria
segments.summary: Factors supporting mass hysteria: war anxiety, a Nazi POW escape nearby, the Journal Gazette headlines, wartime gas fears, no motive, no isolated chemical, and the end coinciding with the stomach-tube policy.

segments.title: Case against mass hysteria
segments.summary: Physical evidence such as the pink cloth, slashed screen, and boot print. Calls to police were below average, which may explain the quiet. Johnson excluded men and children and could not interview victims psychologically. The attacks did not overlap geographically or in time.

segments.title: Scott Marona and Farley Llewellyn theory
segments.summary: Scott Marona's book The Mad Gasser of Mattoon names Farley Llewellyn, a chemist who built a lab that exploded, as the culprit. Marona suggests nitromethane and says Llewellyn's sisters may have covered for him. Locals described Llewellyn as an outsider, and the hosts note the evidence is unverified.

segments.title: Nitromethane and Llewellyn critique
segments.summary: Nitromethane matches many symptoms but is known more for explosions. The hosts discuss problems with Marona's sourcing, the lack of state hospital records, and the speculative nature of the claims.

segments.title: Closing remarks and Matchbox toy
segments.summary: No one knows who the mad gasser was. Chuck shows a Matchbox Monster in My Pocket figure of the Mad Gasser, and the hosts close the live show.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing credits and iHeartRadio production note.
